items.title: Supply and Demand
items.content:
“For fifty years I’ve been doing this. I can’t remember a period where I had less clarity on where we’re going to be in 12 months — Stan Druckenmiller 
 I spent a few days in Austin last week at the TomorrowX investment conference. Its theme was AI – what else – yet while the mood in the room was upbeat, havoc was playing out in markets. Unmoved by the leather-clad executives strutting the stage, the Nasdaq lost 10% of its value over the week, before Jensen Huang’s return prompted a recovery. 1 
 CEOs of financial firms reckon that such volatility is to be expected. “Whenever there’s a technology acceleration, people imagine a growth curve,” said David Solomon of Goldman Sachs. “And then as more information comes to fruition, they recalibrate that growth curve. Right now we’re going through a recalibration of that growth curve. But that still doesn’t mean that people have it exactly right.”
 “There’s definitely high bubble alert in the markets,” said Jon Gray of Blackstone. “People are very focused on this and I think skepticism when you have this kind of investment boom and technological transformation is healthy. And you have to concede that there will be misallocations of capital… But I think the negativity has gone too far in aggregate.”
 Both of them point to an upsurge in demand for AI services. Gray revealed that Blackstone portfolio companies are spending 20 times more on models. Others gave similarly bullish updates on AI usage at their organisations. Tony Xu of Doordash said AI spend there went up 20 times this year. Lin Qiao of Fireworks AI, a startup that helps companies run, ensemble and train their own open-weight models, said that enterprise token consumption is up 12 times in six months. Brian Armstrong of Coinbase said that his personal AI spend has gone from about $500 a week to about $5,000 a week. And AlphaSense, a market intelligence platform, disclosed that its annualized token usage hit 75 trillion in October, up 12-fold from a year earlier (ahem, I may be behind some of that).
 The trouble is that amid improved compute efficiency, higher volumes don’t necessarily flow into higher lab revenues. That’s clear from Ramp’s data on AI token spending by businesses that use its spend management software. Token volume is still going up – in the four weeks to November 15, it was 27% higher than in the previous four weeks – but spending rose by only 8%.
 As an early adopter, Doordash is a case in point. “I think we were single digit customer number for OpenAI,” says Xu. Now, though, he concedes that spend has plateaued as frontier models have become more efficient and as Doordash has shifted some of its workload to open-weight models that it fine-tunes itself.
 This all matters because the massive investment in infrastructure underway needs revenues to fund it. Assuming investors demand a 10% return, the industry would need to generate about $3.5 trillion a year of revenue, once the buildout is complete, to justify the nearly $9 trillion being spent on US data centres due to open by 2032. That assumes two-thirds of the money goes on chips with a six-year life, the rest on buildings and power lasting 20 years, and a 50% cash margin. Even if we stretch the useful life of chips out to ten years, revenue of $2.7 trillion would still be required ( paid subscribers can play with these numbers in a spreadsheet here ).
 Yet based on their third quarters, Anthropic and OpenAI together only generate around $108 billion of annualized revenue – so we’re a long way short.
 Nor are users themselves adding to the pie through economic gains of their own. Productivity improvements have been so far elusive. Beyond the tech sector, revenue per worker inside America’s largest public companies remains broadly flat , as do profit margins. “The benefits aren’t observable in our current quarterly earnings,” admitted JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum on his latest earnings call.
 But there are several reasons to heed the buzz on the Austin stage. To find out what they are, and why lenders rather than demand are now setting the pace of the AI buildout, read on.

items.title: A Banker’s Guide to Anthropic
items.content:
Reminder: I’m on stage at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin next week, and then at Fintech Nerdcon in San Diego. I’ll then be in New York. If you want to catch up, please get in touch. 
 When Anthropic lists on the stock market next week, the money it raises will be just the start. Through its IPO, Anthropic plans to raise as much as $100 billion. Leveraged up, though, that can go much further.
 So far, Anthropic has refrained from tapping the corporate bond market. As a young start-up burning billions of dollars a year on an untested business model, it would hardly have had a look-in. Instead, it has relied on equity investors and on suppliers, who together have put in more than $140 billion.
 But with a Nasdaq listing and a cash pile of $212 billion, its charms are harder to resist. In the run-up, it already secured a $15 billion revolving credit facility from banks managing its IPO. The bigger prize is the bond market. Shortly after its own IPO in June, SpaceX raised $25 billion of senior unsecured bonds. Anthropic’s bankers would like to follow.
 To do that on good terms, it needs a credit rating, specifically an investment-grade one. Its bankers, Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, have been lobbying Moody’s and S&P to grant one as soon as it lists. A rating of BBB– or higher would open Anthropic up to the $13 trillion global investment-grade market, and the insurers and pension funds that dominate it.
 Suppliers have a vested interest, too. When we discussed it in The Art of Doing Financial Engineering , Broadcom had agreed to stand behind $30 billion of debt raised to buy hardware leased to Anthropic. Last month, a second deal took its commitments to more than $70 billion. Broadcom would like to share the load. “It’s an open secret, Anthropic is well on its way to an IPO, and with that, its investment credit will change,” chief executive officer Hock Tan told analysts. An investment-grade rating would let future financings rest on Anthropic’s own credit, rather than its suppliers’.
 Even the revolver hinges on it: for now the facility is secured, but the collateral falls away – and the pricing improves – once two of the three major agencies call Anthropic investment grade.
 One agency reckons it’s there. AIR Platforms is an AI-native credit intelligence and risk-scoring startup founded by Moody’s and Goldman Sachs veterans. It rates Anthropic BBB, two notches above OpenAI. Sadly for the company, AIR Platforms is not a “nationally recognized statistical rating organization” so it doesn’t count. Kroll Bond Rating Agency, which is, rates Anthropic BB+. Blackstone, which marketed the latest Broadcom-backed deal, thinks a rating in the BB range is more likely once the IPO is done.
 Key to the outcome is Anthropic’s cash flow profile. A $1.4 trillion market cap would be nice, and would give comfort to lenders, but it can’t be used to repay debt: you need free cash flow for that. To see how Anthropic plans to pay for close to $1 trillion of commitments, and who is lending it the money, read on.

items.title: The Insatiable Demand for Alpha
items.content:
Reminder: I’ll be attending the TomorrowX Summit in Austin later this month, followed by Fintech Nerdcon in San Diego. If you’re at either, please say hi. 
 In 1969, a year after oil was discovered in Prudhoe Bay, the state of Alaska ran an auction to sell drilling rights along its Arctic coastline. Oil companies flocked to bid, paying up a total of $900 million. For Alaska, this was a massive windfall, equivalent to five times its annual budget. Lawmakers debated what to do with all the cash.
 It took seven years to settle on a plan. So that future generations could benefit, they would set up a permanent fund, to remain out of reach of day-to-day government spending, with the goal of generating income into perpetuity. It required a constitutional change, which in turn required a referendum, but eventually they resolved to invest at least 25% of its oil and mineral royalties into a fund. This week marks the 50th anniversary of the launch of that fund.
 Today, the Alaska Permanent Fund has assets of $88 billion. It’s not as big as Norway’s oil fund, which we discussed some time ago, but it’s the closest America has to a sovereign wealth fund. Each year, the state is allowed to draw 5% from the fund to finance government services and to pay a dividend to residents. This year, eligible residents will each receive a check for $1,200.
 Initially , the fund was invested entirely in bonds. It wasn’t until 1983 that it diversified into stocks and real estate, though allocations remained low for a long time. In 1999, its mandate was broadened to allow a 5% allocation to alternative investments and, in 2004, the fund made its first foray into hedge funds.
 At first, hedge fund investments were made through a fund-of-funds program. Alaska hired three managers to select hedge funds on its behalf but performance was disappointing. In the ten years through to 2016, those hedge funds generated a 3.4% annualized return, weighed by two down years, and provided little protection against market drawdowns. The double fees linked to the fund-of-funds structure contributed a further drag.
 In 2016, under Marcus Frampton, now its chief investment officer, the fund changed its approach to bring hedge fund selection in-house. “We only wanted managers that had a track record of making money in down markets,” he explained . One of his most significant allocations was to Millennium Management. In summer 2018, members of Millennium’s capital development team made the trek to Juneau to meet Frampton and two colleagues and early the following year, they invested $300 million.
 Alaska was lucky to get in. Millennium “has been closed forever and then reopens periodically,” Greg Allen of Callan Associates told its board of trustees. In late 2019, it had an opportunity to add, though it would mean lifting a cap on individual hedge fund allocations. At the beginning of 2020, the fund invested a further $80 million, making it the largest holding in its hedge fund portfolio.
 The shift in approach paid off. Alaska now allocates to 18 managers, accounting for 8% of its total portfolio. When markets slid in 2022, the hedge fund part of its portfolio was up about 8%. In the nine years since the restructuring, the average annualized return of the hedge fund portfolio has been 6.7% with no down years and a low correlation to overall markets. Frampton is happy.
 In fact, he’s so happy that he would like to do more. “If you put our absolute return numbers into the optimizer, it would say put half the portfolio in it, because we’re getting CPI plus five there, totally uncorrelated.” The problem, though, is that “the more money we push into absolute return, the harder it is to get that really special return because the good funds are capacity constrained.”
 Perhaps Millennium has an answer to that. When Alaska first invested, Millennium was a $35 billion fund; it is now knocking on the door of $100 billion. Its return in October was weak , down 2.3%, but that sits within its risk tolerance limits and compared with other funds, it could have been worse. How it performs in November, when many funds have struggled, will be key. “I have covered hedge funds for nearly 16 years, and I can’t remember a day like today,” posted Bloomberg correspondent Nishant Kumar this week.
 If Millennium can outperform the turmoil, it will validate Frampton’s thinking and as it scales up, that will allow more allocators to participate. To see what Millennium is up to, read on.

items.title: Follow the Money
items.content:
Something a bit different this week. I’ve been doing a lot of presenting recently, so I thought I’d share my materials with paid subscribers. Net Interest has been running for over six years now, and with 300+ issues, the archive has become a trove of analysis and commentary on the financial sector. My AI agents had a field day with it. They sorted every post by theme, tracked how the focus has shifted over time and pulled the key data and quotes into one place. Then they went back to the original sources to bring the numbers up to date.
 The result is the deck attached below. It elaborates on seven themes:
 AI is a financing story. Long-time readers know I like to find the bank inside every company. AI has a whole ecosystem of them: labs like Anthropic that commit long to earn short, lessors like CoreWeave that rely on the capital markets for their business model, and guarantors like Nvidia, the Fannie/Freddie of compute.
 Private markets are the new public markets. Built for patient institutional capital, private markets are increasingly underpinned by retail savers, life insurers and banks. New pockets of demand grow the pie, but they also introduce new risks.
 Banks and the credit cycle. Consumer sentiment hit its lowest level on record this year, yet banks keep lending and credit remains benign.
 AI and the work of finance. Financial services companies thrive on customer inattention. Could AI agents, with their infinite attention spans, be their downfall? 
 Markets for everyone. Retail investors used to be dismissed as the dumb money. Now they’re a structural force, from index options in India to prediction markets in the US. Exchanges are racing to keep up.
 The battleground in payments. Payments has emerged as one of the most competitive segments of finance. Upstarts are coming for the incumbents that once tried to buy them, tech giants are deciding how far into finance they want to go, and stablecoins promise to rebuild the rails from scratch.
 People, risk and succession. For an industry that runs on numbers, finance still depends heavily on individuals. Who takes over from Jamie Dimon, how Ken Griffin manufactures talent, and why the biggest asset managers prefer to stay private all come down to people.
 Each section draws on posts from the archive, and there’s a reading list at the end if you want to go deeper. Feel free to use it – and let me know what you think.
